newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica deals casino permits, firms aim at jackpot.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica deals casino permits, firms aim at jackpot.

text.p: South Africa has granted its first ever legal gaming licences for three new casino complexes and industry figures said on Wednesday they were looking to apply for more.

Apartheid-era laws forbade gaming houses, forcing entreprenuers like Sun City-founder Sol Kerzner to build Las Vegas-style resorts in the former black homelands, where the white-ruled government allowed more relaxed rules.
But on Tuesday the northern province of Mpumalanga became the first South African region to name preferred bidders for three new casinos.

Tsogo Sun, a joint-venture between a black consortium and South African Breweries hotels unit Southern Sun, has been selected for resorts in the cities of Witbank and Nelspruit, while Global Resorts has been chosen for Secunda.
Tsogo chief executive Jabu Mabuza told Reuters his group was already keeping an eye out for other provinces to offer licences and try to tap into the potentially huge market for gaming.
"We see ourselves as a player that is going to apply for licences throughout the country," he said.
Mabuza said he thought it was likely that Gauteng -- South Africa's most populous region containing Johannesburg and Pretoria -- would be the next to tender for applications.
KwaZulu-Natal and Western Cape would probably follow soon after, he added.

The only thing standing in the way of Tsogo and Global Resorts from starting work on their gambling palaces is a routine probity investigation by the Mpumalanga Gaming Board, which is scheduled to finish by the end of March.
The South African industry looks like a prize worth bidding for. Consultants Ersnt & Young have valued existing casino spending in the country at four billion rand a year.
The eagerness to get started is shown by the fact that Tsogo plans to open two temporary casinos on the sites of its planned complexes by July.

Tsogo aims to build a 360 million rand resort at Witbank and a 320 million rand one at Nelspruit. The complexes will have hotels, restaurants and shops as well as the all-important casinos. Construction should take about a year.
Global Resorts plans a 200 million rand resort at Secunda.
The South African government is also keen to get the industry kick-started after long delays to a National Gambling Act were overcome last year.

The legislation standardises South African law after the black homelands were incorporated back into the newly democratic country following the 1994 elections which created a hotch-potch of different gambling laws and venues.
A successful industry will provide the government with much-needed tax revenues.

Mpumalanga, which still has one more licence to award, says it cannot calculate exactly the benefits the industry will bring to the province's economy, but that they are likely to be large, including the creation of about 4,000 permanent jobs.
"The spin-offs are so wide that it is difficult to put any final figure on it," said Andre Wilsenach, the Gaming Board's chief executive.
